newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RUGBY UNION-NZ'S FITZPATRICK KEEN FOR WORLD SERIES.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-NZ'S FITZPATRICK KEEN FOR WORLD SERIES.

text.p: All Black captain Sean Fitzpatrick believes rugby union should be globalised with a world competition that would help northern hemisphere teams to catch up with their southern counterparts.
"I think the northern hemisphere would be the first to admit that they're a bit behind," the inspirational All Black hooker told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"To have a Five Nations of the three southern hemisphere teams and the British Lions and say France would be a wonderful competition." New Zealand, South Africa and Australia are currently considered the top three rugby playing nations in the world.
The former British colonies have long been renowned for their big, strong men in the forwards, and much of their rugby dominance is due to their strength in the scrum.
But the southern sides have also rapidly adapted to the professional era, patenting a fast, expansive, crowd-pleasing style of rugby in recent years which the northern teams have yet to emulate.
The New Zealand All Blacks won the inaugural World Cup in 1987, the Australian Wallabies won in 1991, and South Africa's Springboks edged out New Zealand to take coveted crown in 1995.
Fitzpatrick said the split between the northern and southern hemisphere rugby nations was evident in the current British Lions tour of South Africa.

"I must say I've been very impressed with the Lions, especially in the backs and the way they're trying to do things. But they'd have to have a concern in the forwards," he said. "To win rugby over there you definitely have to be able to compete at scrum time and they seem to be under a bit of pressure there."
Fitzpatrick, who led the All Blacks to their first ever series win in South Africa last year, said the Lions currently lacked the set-piece play to beat the reigning World Champions.
"The South Africans are very difficult to beat at home, and they've learnt a lot from last year. The Lions would be the first to admit that it's going to be difficult to win a series over there."
Fitzpatrick suggested the northern teams could start playing during their summer to coincide with the southern rugby season.

"Maybe they (the northern hemisphere) have to start playing rugby in the summer, or we do that down here. But it would make more sense if they started playing rugby in our winter to globalise the game," he said.
The idea of a global competition was last aired in 1995, when many leading rugby players were linked to the failed World Rugby Corporation's bid to overhaul the sport's worldwide structure.
Fitzpatrick conceded the prospects for a world competition in the immediate future were slim.
"It's a matter of the IRB (Intenational Rugby Board) coming to agreement in terms of sorting the calendar out, but I can't see it in the near future," he said.

The 34-year-old veteran of 83 tests was named on Sunday to lead the All Blacks for the sixth year in succession as they embark on a demanding 12-test match itinerary in 1997, kicking off with a test against Fiji on Saturday.
They will play two tests against Argentina, two against South Africa, three against Australia, two against England, one against Wales and one against Ireland.
